1023.title: Going home
1023.hook: John Muir: going to the mountains is going home
1023.carry: nature's peace will flow into you
1023.howItsDone: Some people on a personal spiritual path treat time in wild country, a hike, a hill, a long view, as a regular practice of return, and Muir's writing is often read along the way.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Emerson on a muddy common, and the transparent eye-ball. Your line was nothing, seeing all. Did you take ten steps without the commentary? A new week starts today, and it starts in the mountains. Day one thousand twenty-three.

"Thousands of tired, nerve-shaken, over-civilized people are beginning to find out that going to the mountains is going home". John Muir wrote that line in a book called Our National Parks. Tired. Nerve-shaken. Over-civilized. It reads like a description of a crowded commute, or a long day of screens. And when Muir looked at worn-out city people heading for the hills, he didn't call it a getaway. He called it a homecoming.
screen: `TIRED, NERVE-SHAKEN, OVER-CIVILIZED.` → `HEADING FOR THE HILLS.` → `NOT A GETAWAY.`

segments.voice: Four turns in Muir's thought. First, the diagnosis. Over-civilized is a funny word, and a sharp one. In this sentence he doesn't attack towns. He's naming a kind of tiredness that comes from too much indoors, too much noise, too little sky. Second, the reversal. Ordinary talk about trips says the mountains are where you go away to. Muir flips it. The mountains are home, and the rest is the trip. Whatever people lose in the crowded streets, he suggests, they get back where the land is open. Third, wildness as need, not luxury. His sentence keeps going: "that wildness is a necessity; and that mountain parks and reservations are useful not only as fountains of timber and irrigating rivers, but as fountains of life." Timber and water are useful. Muir adds a third use you can't measure in boards or gallons: life itself. Fourth, what the mountains give. In the same book he writes: "Climb the mountains and get their good tidings. Nature's peace will flow into you as sunshine flows into trees." Good tidings is the King James Bible's phrase for good news, and some readers hear an echo of it here. For him, the high country preaches. Its message isn't a doctrine. It's peace, freshness, and cares, he says, dropping off "like autumn leaves." Last week, poets and thinkers stood still and looked. Muir takes a step. He walks into the awe and calls it home.
screen: `TIRED AND OVER-CIVILIZED` · `GOING HOME, NOT AWAY` · `WILDNESS IS A NECESSITY` · `THE GOOD TIDINGS OF THE MOUNTAINS` · then, large: `GOING HOME.`

segments.voice: The practice is to look at a hill or a horizon. If you can see one, a ridge, a rooftop line, a distant tree, the far end of a street, let your eyes rest there. If you can't, close your eyes and remember a place in open country that felt like yours. Let your gaze go long. Let your shoulders drop. With each slow breath out, let one small care go, the way a leaf lets go of a branch. The bell holds the time.
Going home. John Muir's name for going to the mountains: not leaving real life behind, but coming back to it. Today's word.
Your line: nature's peace will flow into you. Sometime today, find the farthest thing you can see, out a window or down a street, and look at it for a few breaths. Day one thousand twenty-three.

what a scholar hears: the sentence runs on as a chain, going home, wildness a necessity, parks as "fountains of life", and later he calls what the mountains give "good tidings", the King James Bible's phrase for good news.

1024.title: Grandeur in this view
1024.hook: Darwin ends the Origin: there is grandeur in this view of life
1024.howItsDone: Some people on a personal spiritual path, religious and not, read the last paragraph of the Origin as a meditation on life, and practice slow, close looking at living things in gardens, parks and overgrown corners.

segments.voice: Yesterday, John Muir and the mountains. Your line was nature's peace will flow into you. Did you find the farthest thing you could see? Today, a naturalist kneels, in words at least, beside a weedy bank. Day one thousand twenty-four.

A bank of earth, overgrown. Weeds tangled together, birds in the bushes, insects in the air, worms working in the wet soil. Nobody would put it on a postcard. But it's the picture Charles Darwin chose for the last paragraph of On the Origin of Species: "It is interesting to contemplate an entangled bank, clothed with many plants of many kinds, with birds singing on the bushes, with various insects flitting about, and with worms crawling through the damp earth". From that muddy bank, he builds to his final sentence. And its key word is grandeur.
screen: `AN OVERGROWN BANK.` → `NOT A POSTCARD.` → `HIS LAST PARAGRAPH.`

segments.voice: Here is how the book ends: "There is grandeur in this view of life, with its several powers, having been originally breathed into a few forms or into one; and that, whilst this planet has gone cycling on according to the fixed law of gravity, from so simple a beginning endless forms most beautiful and most wonderful have been, and are being, evolved." Four things to hear. First, the entangled bank. Darwin's awe doesn't start with a mountain or a galaxy. It starts with weeds and worms, ordinary life, crowded together in the dirt. Second, grandeur. It's a word for size and splendor, the kind people use for palaces and mountains. Darwin spends it on weeds and worms, and on the long process that made them. Third, two clocks at once. The planet goes "cycling on" by a fixed law, round and round. Meanwhile life does something else entirely: it branches, from a simple beginning into "endless forms most beautiful and most wonderful." One steady circle, one endless unfolding. Fourth, the tense. "Have been, and are being, evolved." Not finished. Still happening, on the bank, in the garden, now. People read this sentence in very different ways. Some people of faith hear in it the wonder of creation still at work. Some people with no faith at all hear wonder enough in the process itself. Darwin's sentence makes room for both readers. And both can stand on the same muddy bank and say the same word.
screen: `AN ENTANGLED BANK` · `GRANDEUR FOR WEEDS AND WORMS` · `FROM SO SIMPLE A BEGINNING` · `STILL BEING EVOLVED` · then, large: `GRANDEUR IN THIS VIEW.`

segments.voice: The practice is to look at a living thing's design. A leaf, a houseplant, an insect on the window, a pet, or your own hand. Choose one, and look at how it's put together. Where it branches. Where it joins. How one part fits another. Don't name the parts. Just follow them with your eyes, slowly, the way you'd follow a path. When your attention drifts, come back to the next joint, the next curve. The bell holds the time.
Entangled bank. Darwin's image for ordinary life, weeds and worms, from which he saw grandeur: life branching, from so simple a beginning, into endless forms. Today's word.
Your line: endless forms most beautiful. Find one tangled, overlooked patch of life today, a weedy corner, a crack in a wall, and give it a full look. Day one thousand twenty-four.

1025.title: The mysterious
1025.hook: Einstein wrote that the most beautiful thing we can experience is the mysterious
1025.howItsDone: Some people on a personal spiritual path, religious and not, keep a practice of sitting with an open question rather than an answer, and Einstein's essay is often read as a description of that kind of wonder.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Darwin's entangled bank, and the last word of his book. Your line was endless forms most beautiful. Did you find a tangled corner of life? Today, a physicist names what he thinks is worth the most. Day one thousand twenty-five.

What's the most beautiful thing a person can experience? Ask around and the answers come quickly. A newborn's face. A sunrise over water. Falling in love. A piece of music that stops you halfway up the stairs. A friend laughing at the kitchen table. Albert Einstein, the physicist, gave a different answer in an essay about what he believed. He said the most beautiful thing we can experience is the mysterious. Not the solved. The mysterious.
screen: `THE MOST BEAUTIFUL THING?` → `A PHYSICIST'S ANSWER.` → `NOT THE SOLVED.`

segments.voice: His words are paraphrased here, not quoted. First, the claim itself. The most beautiful thing we can experience, Einstein wrote, is the mysterious. Not a puzzle waiting for an answer key. Something real that we can sense but can't get to the bottom of. Second, where it leads. He called it the source of all true art and all true science. That's a surprise from a scientist. Plenty of people picture science as a machine for getting rid of mystery. He says the opposite: mystery is where the work begins, and where it keeps coming from. Third, what happens without it. Einstein wrote that a person to whom this feeling is a stranger, who can no longer pause to wonder and stand rapt in awe, is as good as dead: their eyes are closed. Strong words. Fourth, his religion. He went on to say that knowing something we can't penetrate exists, a deep reason and a radiant beauty that our minds can only grasp in their most basic forms, is at the heart of true religiousness. And then he drew a careful line: in that sense, and in that sense only, he counted himself among the devoutly religious. He was naming his own meaning of the word, not setting a rule for anyone else's.
screen: `THE MOST BEAUTIFUL THING` · `THE SOURCE OF ART AND SCIENCE` · `EYES THAT CAN STILL WONDER` · `RELIGIOUS IN THIS SENSE ONLY` · then, large: `THE MYSTERIOUS.`

segments.voice: The practice is to sit with one mystery. Choose something you can't explain and probably never will. Why a piece of music can move someone to tears. What another person's inner life is really like. Why the world can be understood at all. Hold it the way you'd hold a stone in your palm. Don't try to solve it. When the mind starts arguing, set the argument down, and go back to simply holding the question. The bell holds the time.
The mysterious. Einstein's name for what we sense but can't get to the bottom of, which he called the most beautiful thing we can experience. Today's word.
Your line: stand rapt in awe. Today, look once at a face you know well, and notice how much of that person you still can't see. Day one thousand twenty-five.

1026.title: Star stuff
1026.hook: Carl Sagan: we are made of star stuff
1026.carry: the cosmos has a way to know itself
1026.howItsDone: Some people on a personal spiritual path, religious and not, use Sagan's picture of star stuff as a short contemplation on the body, often looking at a hand or feeling the pulse while recalling where its materials came from.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Einstein and the most beautiful thing we can experience. Your line was stand rapt in awe. Did a familiar face turn out to hold more than you could see? Today, the awe comes right down to your own body. Day one thousand twenty-six.

The nearest object to you right now is probably your own hand. Skin, knuckles, the faint lines on the palm, the blue of a vein at the wrist. It goes everywhere you go, and it is easy to stop seeing it. The astronomer Carl Sagan, in his television series and book Cosmos, said something about what that hand is made of, something that sounds like poetry but was meant as plain fact. We are made, he said, of star stuff.
screen: `THE NEAREST THING: A HAND.` → `A FAMILIAR THING.` → `MADE OF STAR STUFF.`

segments.voice: Sagan's words are paraphrased here, not quoted. First, the claim. In Cosmos, Sagan explained that the nitrogen in our DNA, the calcium in our teeth, the iron in our blood, even the carbon in an apple pie, were made inside stars. Much of what our bodies are built from was forged in stars and scattered when they died. Second, what that does to distance. Pascal, at the start of last week, looked at the stars and felt the silence of the infinite spaces. Sagan looks at the same stars and sees family. The sky isn't only out there. Some of it is here, in the hand nearest you. Third, the next step. Sagan went further. He said that through us, the cosmos has a way to know itself. The stuff of stars, put together as a person, now looks back up at the stars and wonders where it came from. Fourth, a neighbor's line. The Bible has its own saying about what a person is made of. In Genesis, God tells Adam: "for dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return." That's a different teaching, from a different source, and Sagan wasn't quoting it. But some readers hold the two side by side: dust, and star stuff. Both say a person is made of the stuff of the world, and some readers hear in both a call to humility, and to wonder.
screen: `MADE INSIDE STARS` · `THE SKY IS ALSO HERE` · `THE COSMOS KNOWING ITSELF` · `DUST THOU ART` · then, large: `STAR STUFF.`

segments.voice: The practice is to look at your hand. Rest it, palm up, in your lap or on a table. Look at it the way you'd look at something you've never seen. The lines. The color. The pulse, if you can find it at the wrist. Let the thought come once, without forcing it: much of this was made inside stars. Then just keep looking, and breathing. The bell holds the time.
Star stuff. Carl Sagan's phrase for what we're made of: materials made inside stars, now able to look back up and wonder. Today's word.
Your line: the cosmos has a way to know itself. Every time you wash your hands today, give them one look, and let the line come back. Day one thousand twenty-six.

1027.title: The numinous
1027.hook: Rudolf Otto named the holy as a mystery that makes us tremble and draws us in (The Idea of the Holy)
1027.howItsDone: Students of religion use Rudolf Otto's word numinous for the sense of a holy presence that is both overwhelming and attractive; some people who practice no religion use it for moments in nature or music that feel too large for ordinary words.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Carl Sagan. Your line was the cosmos has a way to know itself. Where did that line find you? Today a scholar of religion tries to name the feeling underneath all this awe. Day one thousand twenty-seven.
screen: `THE COSMOS HAS A WAY TO KNOW ITSELF.`

segments.voice: A storm rolls in after dark. The power cuts out. Lightning shows the whole street for half a second, then nothing. Some people pull the curtains shut. Others drift to the window, a little scared, and can't stop looking. Back away, come closer, both in the same body at the same moment. Rudolf Otto, a scholar of religion, wrote a whole book about that double pull. He thought it sat near the heart of what people mean when they call something holy. And he decided the old words weren't good enough for it. He needed a new one.
screen: `THE STORM AT THE WINDOW.` → `BACK AWAY, COME CLOSER.` → `A NEW WORD FOR THE HOLY.`

segments.voice: Otto's book is called The Idea of the Holy. First, his complaint. When people say holy, he noticed, they often just mean perfectly good. Otto thought that leaves something out: something stranger than goodness, a sense of a presence that is wholly other. He wanted a word for that part alone, so he made one. From the Latin numen, a word for divine power or presence, he formed numinous. Second, he said the numinous can't be strictly defined. It can only be pointed at until the listener recognizes it, the way you'd help someone recognize a smell. So he gave it a Latin description: mysterium tremendum et fascinans. Mysterium: a mystery, beyond our grasp. Tremendum: something to tremble before, so overwhelming it makes a person feel small. He called that creature-feeling. Third, the half that's easy to miss: fascinans. Fascinating. Drawing you in. For Otto the holy doesn't only frighten. It attracts. The trembling and the drawing near arrive together. Fourth, an old scene that holds both halves. In the book of Exodus, Moses sees a bush burning that doesn't burn up, and in the King James words he says, "I will now turn aside, and see this great sight." He walks toward it. A moment later, "Moses hid his face; for he was afraid to look upon God." Toward, and away. Otto was a Christian theologian, and readers argue about his theology. But the word he made has traveled far beyond his book. A storm, a birth, the sea at night, a silence in a very old room: some moments ask for a bigger word than nice. Numinous is one.
screen: `HOLY MEANS MORE THAN GOOD.` · `POINTED AT, NOT DEFINED.` · `TREMENDUM AND FASCINANS.` · `MOSES TURNS ASIDE, THEN HIDES.` · then, large: `MYSTERIUM TREMENDUM ET FASCINANS.`

segments.voice: Settle, and let the breath slow. Bring back one moment that made you tremble: not danger alone, but something too big. A storm. A newborn. The ocean after dark. A piece of music. A silence in an old building. Stay inside that moment. Was there a part of you that wanted to step back? Was there a part that wanted to step closer? Let both be there, if they were. Don't explain the moment. Just stand in it again. If you pray, you can bring it into your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Numinous. Rudolf Otto's word for the holy as a mystery that makes us tremble and draws us in. Today's word.
Your line: tremble and draw near. Today, when something stops you, a sky, a sound, a face, don't hurry past it. Take one step closer. Day one thousand twenty-seven.

1028.title: The varieties
1028.hook: William James described mystical experience as hard to put into words, yet felt as knowledge (The Varieties of Religious Experience)
1028.howItsDone: Readers of William James use his marks of mystical experience, especially ineffability and the noetic quality, to talk about religious and nonreligious experiences alike; some people keep a journal to try to put such moments into words.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rudolf Otto's word, numinous. Your line was tremble and draw near. Did something stop you long enough to take that one step closer? Day one thousand twenty-eight.

"So how was it?" Someone asks after the birth, the funeral, the night on the mountain, the concert where the whole room went quiet. And the answer comes out thin. "It was... amazing. You kind of had to be there." The speaker knows that's not it. The listener knows that's not it. Something real happened, and the words came back nearly empty. An American psychologist and philosopher, William James, took that awkward moment seriously. He gathered people's own accounts of their biggest experiences and noticed the same stumble again and again.
screen: `SO HOW WAS IT?` → `YOU HAD TO BE THERE.` → `JAMES COLLECTS THE STUMBLES.`

segments.voice: His book is called The Varieties of Religious Experience. Varieties, plural, on purpose: James wasn't defending one church or attacking another. He filled the pages with first-person letters and memoirs from very different people, and then asked what they had in common. First, the mark he called ineffability. The person who has the experience says it defies expression. No report in words seems adequate. James compared it to music or to love: to know it, it seems you have to have been there. Second, the surprise. You'd expect something that can't be put into words to feel vague. James said these states feel the opposite. He called that their noetic quality: they seem to the person to be knowledge. Insight. Something learned, not just felt, and it often carries a sense of authority for a long time after. Hard to say, and yet known. Third, James's honesty about himself. He admitted his own temperament kept him almost entirely out of such states. He was writing about them from the outside, carefully, without mocking and without claiming more than he'd seen. Fourth, a neighbor who said it long before him. The Tao Te Ching, the Chinese classic that tradition credits to Laozi, opens, in James Legge's translation: "The Tao that can be trodden is not the enduring and unchanging Tao." The Way itself is what the words keep missing. That doesn't make the words useless. It makes them honest when they stumble.
screen: `VARIETIES, ON PURPOSE.` · `INEFFABLE: IT DEFIES EXPRESSION.` · `NOETIC: IT FEELS LIKE KNOWING.` · `JAMES WRITES FROM THE OUTSIDE.` · then, large: `HARD TO SAY, AND YET KNOWN.`

segments.voice: Settle, and let the breath slow. Pick one big moment of your own, any kind. Now try to describe it, silently, in three or four sentences, as if to a friend. Go slowly. Notice exactly where the words start to slip: the sentence that comes out flatter than the thing itself. Don't fix it. Stay at the edge where the words run out, and just keep the moment there with you. If you pray, you can let the unspoken part be your prayer. The bell holds the time.
The varieties. William James's study of religious experience: moments that are hard to put into words, and yet feel like knowledge. Today's word.
Your line: hard to say. Today, when someone tells you about something big and stumbles, don't rush them. Let the stumble be part of the story. Day one thousand twenty-eight.

1029.title: Radical amazement
1029.hook: Abraham Joshua Heschel called for radical amazement at the ordinary (God in Search of Man)
1029.howItsDone: Readers of Heschel often connect radical amazement to Jewish blessings said over ordinary moments, such as waking, eating bread, or seeing lightning; others take the phrase as an invitation to look again at everyday things.

segments.voice: Yesterday, William James. Your line was hard to say. This week went from mountains and Darwin, to the mysterious and star stuff, to the numinous and the varieties. Big things, mostly. Today a rabbi turns the whole week toward the small. Day one thousand twenty-nine.

A faucet. Turn the handle and clean water comes out, cold or hot, whenever you like. A light switch. A slice of bread. The fact that you woke up this morning and your heart had kept going all night without being asked. None of this makes the news. Most days none of it gets a second look. Abraham Joshua Heschel, a Jewish teacher and rabbi, thought that missing second look was one of the deepest problems a person can have. And he had a name for the cure.
screen: `THE FAUCET. THE SWITCH. THE BREAD.` → `NO SECOND LOOK.` → `HESCHEL NAMES THE CURE.`

segments.voice: The name is radical amazement. It comes from his book God in Search of Man. First, what he meant by it. Not amazement at the unusual: comets, miracles, record-breaking anything. Amazement at the usual. At the plain fact that there is anything at all, instead of nothing. Radical, in the sense of going all the way to the root. Second, what it's up against. Heschel wrote that people grow used to the world, and that taking it for granted is not a small mistake. He went so far as to call indifference to the sublime wonder of living the root of sin. Strong words from a gentle writer. For him, losing wonder wasn't a mood problem. It was a way of going blind. Third, where he found the practice. Heschel stood inside Jewish tradition, which has blessings for ordinary moments: on waking, on eating bread, on seeing lightning, on hearing thunder. He saw blessing as a way of refusing to take things for granted, out loud, many times a day. A much older line in the Psalms has the same posture. In the King James words: "I am fearfully and wonderfully made: marvellous are thy works." Fourth, what it asks of anyone today, religious or not. Not a trip somewhere spectacular. A second look at what's already in your hand. Heschel believed wonder was where awareness of God begins. Others who don't share his faith borrow the phrase anyway, because the ordinary is still sitting there, waiting to be noticed.
screen: `AMAZED AT THE USUAL.` · `INDIFFERENCE IS A KIND OF BLINDNESS.` · `BLESSINGS FOR ORDINARY MOMENTS.` · `A SECOND LOOK AT WHAT'S IN YOUR HAND.` · then, large: `FEARFULLY AND WONDERFULLY MADE.`

segments.voice: Pick up one ordinary thing within reach: a cup, a key, a spoon. Settle, and look at it as if it had just been handed to you for the first time. Who made it? What had to happen for it to be here? Then go one step further, Heschel's step: notice that it exists at all. Let the breath move slowly while you look. If you pray, you can let this looking become a blessing in your own tradition's words. The bell holds the time.
Radical amazement. Abraham Joshua Heschel's phrase for wonder at the ordinary, all the way to the root: that anything is here at all. Today's word.
Your line: fearfully and wonderfully made. Today, choose one thing you use without thinking, the faucet, the stairs, your own breath, and give it a full second look. Day one thousand twenty-nine.

pairs: all the way to the root
at the usual, not the unusual
refusing to take it for granted

myth: radical amazement is wonder at rare, spectacular things
Heschel meant amazement at the usual: that there is anything at all.
Heschel called indifference to the wonder of living the root of sin
for him, losing wonder was a way of going blind, not a passing mood.
Jewish tradition has blessings for ordinary moments
on waking, on eating bread, on seeing lightning, on hearing thunder.

fork.setup: you want more wonder in your life. Heschel is your teacher. where does he send you?
options: back to the ordinary things already around you.
away from the world, to think alone.
fork.reveal: radical amazement is wonder at the usual. the faucet, the bread, the fact that anything exists at all.

trapdoor: what you thought: radical amazement means being very, very impressed.
what it means: wonder at the ordinary, at the plain fact that anything is here at all.
what a scholar hears: Heschel's answer to taking the world for granted, rooted in the Jewish habit of blessing ordinary moments.
